```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
source("../R/_tools.R")

# readr rather than datawizard::data_read(), which reads empty cells as "" rather than NA
housing     <- readr::read_csv("../data/housing_emails.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
names_tab <- readr::read_csv("../data/display_names.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
outcomes  <- readr::read_csv("../data/display_outcomes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
subgroups <- readr::read_csv("../data/display_subgroups.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
power     <- readr::read_csv("../data/display_power.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
curve     <- readr::read_csv("../data/spec_curve.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

# Fixed decimals and a true minus sign, for every number on the page
fmt <- \(x, d = 1) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d) |> sub(pattern = "^-", replacement = "−")
pct <- \(x, d = 1) paste0(fmt(x, d), "%")
pe <- \(p) dplyr::case_when(p < 0.0001 ~ "p < 0.0001", p < 0.001 ~ paste("p =", fmt(p, 4)),
                            .default = paste("p =", fmt(p, 3)))

grp <- \(g, col) names_tab[[col]][names_tab$level == "group" & names_tab$group == g]
nm <- \(n, col) names_tab[[col]][names_tab$level == "name" & names_tab$name == n]
out <- \(o, cn, col) outcomes[[col]][outcomes$outcome == o & outcomes$contrast == cn]
sub_ <- \(start, col) subgroups[[col]][startsWith(subgroups$subgroup, start)]
pw <- \(design, gap) power$power[startsWith(power$design, design) & power$gap_pp == gap]
ref <- datawizard::data_filter(curve, is_reference)
sent_range <- range(names_tab$sent[names_tab$level == "name"])
# The test that the six accounts were equally likely, against the numbers sent
sent_p <- chisq.test(names_tab$sent[names_tab$level == "name"])$p.value
# The smallest gap that the reference comparison reports as significant at 5%:
# the half-width of its 95% interval, from the estimator of the case study
ref_fit <- fit_spec(housing)
sig_threshold <- (ref_fit$ci_high - ref_fit$ci_low) / 2
# A logit coefficient moves a probability by at most a quarter of its value
# (Gelman and Hill 2007, p. 82); 0.098 is the coefficient of the replication
score_max_pp <- 100 * 0.098 / 4
# The share of replies written by officials with Hispanic names, by group of names
official_share <- housing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(reply == 1) |>
  datawizard::data_summary(share = 100 * mean(hispanic_official, na.rm = TRUE), by = "group")
# The delivered emails to white and Hispanic names and their coded replies, for
# the rates quoted in section 3, whose declaration builds them again in view
delivered <- housing |> datawizard::data_filter(group %in% c("white", "hispanic"), !is.na(reply))
coded <- delivered |> datawizard::data_filter(reply == 1, !is.na(named))
# The diagnoses of the simulated experiments of sections 3, 5 and 7, run once by
# companion/_model-outputs/simulate_housing.R
dx <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/sim_housing_diagnosis.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
draws <- readr::read_csv("_model-outputs/sim_housing_draws.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
recovery_dx <- dx |> datawizard::data_filter(set == "recovery")
reply_dx <- dx |> datawizard::data_filter(set == "reply")
power_dx <- dx |> datawizard::data_filter(set == "power")
reply_never <- reply_dx |> datawizard::data_filter(greet_marginal == 0, estimator == "among replies")
reply_always <- reply_dx |> datawizard::data_filter(greet_marginal == 1, estimator == "among replies")
power_10 <- power_dx |> datawizard::data_filter(n_per_group == 181, gap == 0.1)
power_null <- power_dx |> datawizard::data_filter(gap == 0)
```

The Housing and racial bias case study is set here among the field experiments with which sociologists and political scientists measure discrimination. The study on which it rests, presented in full on the [background page](../background.qmd), was conducted by the original authors, who emailed public housing authorities across the United States from six names meant to indicate a white, a Black or a Hispanic applicant [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect]. Taking the design itself as its subject, the module first considers what random assignment secures, what an experiment simulated from a known recipe shows about the estimator and what a name conveys to its reader. The later sections examine why comparing the content of replies needs care, how a randomisation test works, what power has to do with the failed replication of the paper in the SCORE replicability study, what blocking the assignment would have added and what such studies ask of the people whom they study. Every number on the page is computed when the page is built, from the course files in `data/` and the simulation diagnoses stored in `companion/_model-outputs/`, with the code shown for the less familiar ones.

## 1. Audit and correspondence studies {#sec-audits}

An audit study measures discrimination by sending requests that are identical except for one characteristic of the person making them, and by comparing how these requests are answered. In its older form, trained testers who differ in that characteristic apply in person, as in the study of hiring by @Pager2003MarkCriminalRecord, which used matched pairs of testers to measure what a criminal record costs an applicant. In the correspondence study, the form that is now more common, the requests are written, and the characteristic is conveyed by the name on a résumé, a letter or an email. @BertrandMullainathan2004AreEmilyGreg sent résumés that differed only in a name meant to indicate race, and a meta-analysis of field experiments on hiring found no change since 1989 in discrimination against African Americans, with some indication of a decline in discrimination against Latinos [@QuillianEtAl2017MetaanalysisFieldExperiments].

Political scientists adapted the correspondence design to those who hold public office or administer it, sending them emails that ask a simple question. @ButlerBroockman2011PoliticiansRaciallyDiscriminate wrote to state legislators and @WhiteEtAl2015WhatNeedVote to local election officials. The original authors summarise these two studies as finding that "blacks and Hispanics making queries about voting procedures are less likely to receive responses from state legislators and local election officials than whites" (p. 4 of the accepted manuscript, to which the page numbers on this page refer). The original authors' own experiment extends the question to officials who decide access to a scarce public good, the 'street-level bureaucrats' whose discretion was described by @Lipsky1980StreetLevelBureaucracy. Studies of this kind usually measure several outcomes of a single request, recording whether a reply came at all, how quickly it came and what it contained. The claim examined in the course concerns the last of these outcomes, the tone of a reply, measured by whether it opened with the sender's name, and section 5 explains why an outcome of this kind requires more care than the first.

## 2. Random assignment {#sec-randomisation}

"Each housing authority was randomly assigned (via random number generator) to receive an email from one of six different accounts with putatively white, Hispanic, and black names" (p. 8). It is this random assignment that turns a comparison between groups of emails into an estimate of the effect of the name. Since the authorities that received Santiago Martinez and those that received Brett Smith were chosen by chance, the two groups also differ only by chance in every other respect, whether in their size, their communities and their staffing or in how busy their offices were that week. A difference in how the two groups of emails were answered can therefore be read as the effect of the name, with chance as the only rival explanation, and it is chance that a test quantifies.

That the groups differ only by chance can be checked on any characteristic that the emails could not have changed. @tbl-balance compares the three groups on the characteristics recorded in the public file, with a $\chi^2$ test of whether each characteristic is distributed alike across the groups.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-balance
#| tbl-cap: "The emails sent to each group of names, by characteristics that the emails could not have changed: the share of each group with a hard-to-find address, and the share in the top third of each community characteristic, with the p-value of a $\\chi^2$ test that the full distribution of the characteristic is the same in the three groups. Source: `data/housing_emails.csv`."
balance_vars <- c(hard_email = "Hard-to-find address", hispanic_third = "Percent Hispanic, top third",
                  black_third = "Percent Black, top third", pop_third = "Population, top third",
                  poverty_third = "Poverty rate, top third", assessment_third = "HUD assessment, top third")
# dplyr inside the loop, because datawizard does not find the variable of each pass
balance <- purrr::imap(balance_vars, \(label, v) {
  shares <- housing |>
    dplyr::mutate(top = if (v == "hard_email") .data[[v]] == 1 else .data[[v]] == "top") |>
    dplyr::summarise(share = 100 * mean(top, na.rm = TRUE), .by = group)
  share_of <- \(g) pct(shares$share[shares$group == g])
  tibble::tibble(Characteristic = label,
                 White = share_of("white"), Black = share_of("black"), Hispanic = share_of("hispanic"),
                 `χ<sup>2</sup> test` = pe(stats::chisq.test(table(housing$group, housing[[v]]))$p.value))
}) |>
  purrr::list_rbind()
balance |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:5, align = "r")
```

No characteristic comes near a significant difference, as random assignment would lead one to expect. The paper reports a check of the same kind, although without a test, giving for each of the six names the average of each community characteristic, computed from the continuous census values, which are replaced by thirds in the public file (Table SI1, p. 43). The groups also differ in size, the six names having been sent between `r sent_range[1]` and `r sent_range[2]` times, a spread that equal chances would rarely produce (a $\chi^2$ test of equal shares gives p = `r formatC(sent_p, format = "f", digits = 3)`). Given this spread, and since the paper says that "[e]ach housing authority was randomly assigned (via random number generator) to receive an email from one of six different accounts" (p. 8) without stating the chance of each account, the six accounts may not have been equally likely. Unequal groups cost a little precision and nothing else, because every authority was still assigned at random, and, for the same reason, no covariate is needed to remove bias. Adjustment for characteristics that predict the outcome can still narrow the standard error, which is one reason why the specification curve retains three adjustment sets beside the raw difference. Random assignment also leads one to expect that such adjustment will move the estimate itself only a little, since characteristics fixed before the emails were sent are independent of the name, and an adjusted estimate obtained from the same emails can differ from the raw difference only through the chance imbalance of these characteristics between the groups, and only to the extent that each characteristic predicts the outcome. As the [Specification curve](../curve.qmd#shifts) page reports, two of the sets move the estimate by about a point on average and the third, the hard-to-find address alone, by less than a tenth of a point, shifts that appear to bear out this expectation, although part of the shift under the two community sets is attributable to the emails left out by these sets for want of community thirds. The replication went one step further by randomising within each state, so that every state received equal numbers of each group of names, a design examined in section 8.

## 3. Simulating the experiment {#sec-simulation}

Whereas most quantitative pages on this site analyse data that came from the world, the data analysed in this section came from a recipe written in advance, which means that the answer is known before any model is fitted. This inversion, known as fake-data simulation, is a standard habit in applied statistics, and *Regression and Other Stories* uses it constantly, on the argument that fitting models to data whose coefficients you planted yourself is how you learn what your models can and cannot recover [@GelmanEtAl2020RegressionOtherStories]. The same habit underpins classroom practice [@GelmanVehtari2024ActiveStatisticsStories] as well as the literature on workflow, in which experimentation on simulated data is one of the named components of model-building [@GelmanEtAl2026BayesianWorkflow]. The design of the experiment is simple enough to be written down in a few lines. Within that design, this section plants a true gap and recovers it, section 5 breaks the recovery by letting the name change who replies, and section 7 uses recipes of the same kind to count how often studies as large as the original study and the replication find a gap.

The simulations are declared and diagnosed with DeclareDesign [@BlairEtAl2023DeclareDesignDeclareDiagnose], an R package that describes a research design in four parts, called by its authors the model, the inquiry, the data strategy and the answer strategy. The **model** is the recipe, describing the units and how each would respond to each condition, while the **inquiry** is the quantity that the study is meant to learn, its estimand. The **data strategy** specifies how the units are sampled and assigned, and the **answer strategy** is the estimator. Once declared in this way, a design can be run as often as one likes, and the package summarises the runs. The summary reports how far the estimates fall from the estimand on average, how widely those estimates scatter, how often the interval covers the truth and how often the test rejects. The simulations with many draws were run once, in the script `simulate_housing.R` stored in `companion/_model-outputs/` of the source repository, and the page reads the diagnoses written by that script, while every declaration on the page runs when the page is built.

The claim compares the Hispanic and the white names, and the recipe below draws its numbers from the `r format(nrow(delivered), big.mark = ",")` delivered emails sent under those names, as recorded in `housing_emails.csv`. In these data, `r insight::format_value(mean(delivered$reply), as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)` of the authorities replied, and among the coded replies, `r insight::format_value(mean(coded$named[coded$group == "white"]), as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)` of the replies to white names and `r insight::format_value(mean(coded$named[coded$group == "hispanic"]), as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)` of those to Hispanic names opened with the name, yielding a gap of `r insight::format_value(out("named", "hispanic", "b_pp"), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points.

In the first recipe, which plants that gap and nothing else, each authority would reply or not whatever the name, leaving the chance of a reply at the same `r insight::format_value(mean(delivered$reply), as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)` for both. Among the authorities that reply, a white name is greeted by name with the probability observed for white names and a Hispanic name with the probability observed for Hispanic names, while an official who would greet the Hispanic name by name would also greet the white one. Each authority therefore has two potential outcomes, namely the greetings that it would give to each name, of which the experiment reveals one. The names are allocated by complete random assignment to as many emails as in the experiment, and the answer strategy is the estimator used in the case study, the difference in the proportions of named greetings among the replies, with HC2 errors.

```{r}
#| label: declare-recovery
# The delivered emails to white and Hispanic names, whose rates the recipe
# plants, and the replies among them that carry a greeting code
delivered <- housing |> datawizard::data_filter(group %in% c("white", "hispanic"), !is.na(reply))
coded <- delivered |> datawizard::data_filter(reply == 1, !is.na(named))
n_delivered <- nrow(delivered)
n_hispanic <- sum(delivered$group == "hispanic")
reply_all <- mean(delivered$reply)
greet_white <- mean(coded$named[coded$group == "white"])
greet_hisp <- mean(coded$named[coded$group == "hispanic"])

# Z = 1 is a Hispanic name; G_Z_0 and G_Z_1 are the greetings that an authority
# would give a white and a Hispanic name if it replied
recovery <-
  DeclareDesign::declare_model(
    N = n_delivered,
    v = runif(N), u = runif(N),
    R = as.integer(v < reply_all),
    G_Z_0 = as.integer(u < greet_white), G_Z_1 = as.integer(u < greet_hisp)
  ) +
  DeclareDesign::declare_inquiry(gap = mean(G_Z_1[R == 1] - G_Z_0[R == 1])) +
  DeclareDesign::declare_assignment(Z = randomizr::complete_ra(N, m = n_hispanic)) +
  DeclareDesign::declare_measurement(G = fabricatr::reveal_outcomes(G ~ Z)) +
  DeclareDesign::declare_estimator(G ~ Z, .method = estimatr::lm_robust, se_type = "HC2",
                                   subset = R == 1, inquiry = "gap", term = "Z",
                                   label = "among replies")

set.seed(20260731)
DeclareDesign::draw_data(recovery) |> head()
DeclareDesign::run_design(recovery) |>
  datawizard::data_select(select = c("inquiry", "estimand", "estimate", "std.error", "p.value"))
```

The first table presents six simulated authorities with both of their potential greetings, the name assigned to them by the draw and the greeting that the experiment would record. The second table reports one run of the whole design, comprising the planted gap among the authorities that replied in this draw (the estimand), the estimate from the replies, its standard error and its p-value. One run amounts to one experiment, which says nothing yet about the estimator. Although the planted value is known, a single estimate that lands near it, or far from it, could be a matter of luck.

The estimator is judged instead by its behaviour over many runs of the same design, and the script `simulate_housing.R` runs this design 2,000 times:

```r
DeclareDesign::diagnose_design(recovery, sims = 2000)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-recovery
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3.2
#| fig-cap: "The estimates of the gap in named greetings in 2,000 simulated experiments whose recipe plants the gap of the original study and lets the name change nothing else. The burgundy line marks the planted gap, and the dashed line the gap that the original study found. Source: `companion/_model-outputs/sim_housing_draws.csv`."
#| fig-alt: "A bell-shaped histogram of simulated gaps centred on about −20 points and spreading from about −37 to −3 points; the planted gap and the observed gap of the study lie together near its centre."
ggplot2::ggplot(draws, ggplot2::aes(100 * estimate)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, boundary = 0, fill = "#0e3b6a", alpha = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = 100 * recovery_dx$mean_estimand, colour = "#8b1538", linewidth = 0.8) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(xintercept = out("named", "hispanic", "b_pp"), colour = "grey30", linetype = 2) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "estimated gap in named greetings (percentage points)", y = "simulated experiments") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

Over the 2,000 draws the estimates average `r insight::format_value(100 * recovery_dx$mean_estimate, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")` points against a planted gap of `r insight::format_value(100 * recovery_dx$mean_estimand, digits = 2, style_negative = "minus")`, indicating that the estimator is unbiased for this recipe to within the noise of the simulation. The standard deviation of the estimates, `r insight::format_value(100 * recovery_dx$sd_estimate, digits = 2)` points, corresponds to the sampling error of a study of this size, which remains unobservable in any single study. The standard error reported by the case study for its one real estimate, `r insight::format_value(out("named", "hispanic", "se_pp"), digits = 2)` points, is an estimate of that sampling error. The 95% interval covered the planted gap in `r insight::format_value(recovery_dx$coverage, as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)` of the draws, close to the 95% that it promises, while the test rejected a gap of zero in `r insight::format_value(recovery_dx$power, as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)` of them. A real study is one draw from a distribution like this one, and the dashed line marks where the original study fell within it.

Recovery is the first check of any estimator, and it is the check that the course runs implicitly whenever an estimator is called unbiased, although its result holds only for the recipe that was written. Section 5 changes that recipe in the one respect that the case-study data cannot check.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Copy the declaration of `recovery` into your workspace and change one ingredient at a time: halve `n_delivered`, set `greet_hisp` equal to `greet_white`, or lower `reply_all` to a quarter. Diagnose each version with `DeclareDesign::diagnose_design(recovery, sims = 500)` and compare the standard deviation of the estimates, the coverage and the power. Which ingredient changes the bias, and which change only the precision?
:::

## 4. Names as treatments {#sec-names}

In a correspondence study the treatment is a name, and a name conveys to its reader more than one thing about its bearer. The original authors chose names distinctive of each group, relying above all on the surname Martinez for the Hispanic names. The authors also tried to match the ages suggested by the names, explaining why with an earlier study: "Butler and Broockman's (2011) comparison of responses to emails from Deshawn and Jake ... may actually be estimating the causal effect of being a young black male relative to being a white male of unclear age" (p. 10). The original authors were able to match the white and the Black names, but not the Hispanic ones, Santiago and Gabriela among them, since "virtually all distinctively Hispanic names ... peak in the 1990s and 2000s in Social Security Administration data" (p. 10). Santiago and Gabriela may therefore have suggested a younger sender as well as a Hispanic one. @Gaddis2017HowBlackAre demonstrated the wider problem for names meant to indicate Black applicants, some of which readers perceive as Black more often than others, with the result that the findings of an audit may depend on which names stand for a group.

The design meets part of this problem by using two names in each group, one male and one female, and @fig-names presents, for each of the six names, the share of replies that opened with the sender's name.

```{r}
#| label: fig-names
#| fig-cap: "The share of replies with a greeting code that opened with the name of the sender, by name, with 95% Wilson intervals. Source: `data/display_names.csv`."
#| fig-alt: "Dot plot of six names with intervals. Brett, Emily and Tyrone lie near 60%, Shanice near 52%, Gabriela near 46% and Santiago near 37%; the two Hispanic names are drawn in burgundy."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
#| code-fold: true
names_tab |>
  datawizard::data_filter(level == "name") |>
  datawizard::data_modify(hispanic = group == "hispanic", name = stats::reorder(name, named_pct)) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = named_pct, y = name, colour = hispanic)) +
  ggplot2::geom_pointrange(ggplot2::aes(xmin = named_lo, xmax = named_hi), size = 0.4, linewidth = 0.7) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "#1d2733", `TRUE` = "#8b1538"), guide = "none") +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(x, "%")) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(20, 80)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "replies that open with the name of the sender", y = NULL) +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

Both Hispanic names drew fewer named greetings than any other name, `r pct(nm("Santiago", "named_pct"))` of the replies to Santiago and `r pct(nm("Gabriela", "named_pct"))` of those to Gabriela, against `r pct(nm("Brett", "named_pct"))` to Brett and `r pct(nm("Emily", "named_pct"))` to Emily. The gap amounts to `r fmt(sub_("male", "b_pp"))` points between the male names (`r pe(sub_("male", "p"))`) and to `r fmt(sub_("female", "b_pp"))` points between the female names (`r pe(sub_("female", "p"))`). The two gaps agree in direction but differ in size, and a study with a single name in each group could not tell whether a difference belonged to the group or to the name. The replication chose differently, as its preregistration explains: "Rather than using both male and female names we will pick only male names, because the original study did not find a difference based on the gender of the name and by eliminating it as a variable we more narrowly focus on race." The replication also selected its four new names, two meant to indicate a Hispanic and two a white sender, from names whose perception by readers had been tested.

Since the sex of the name was crossed with the group by design, every group comprises a male and a female name in similar numbers, and adjustment for the sex of the name changes the gap very little.

```{r}
#| label: sex-check
frame <- spec_frame(housing, comparison = "white", population = "replies", uncoded = "drop")
with_sex <- stats::lm(y ~ hisp + name_sex, data = frame)
round(100 * stats::coef(with_sex)[["hisp"]], 2)
```

The gap moves from `r fmt(ref$b_pp, 2)` to `r fmt(100 * coef(with_sex)[["hisp"]], 2)` points, which is why the specification menu treats this adjustment as a check rather than as an answer in its own right. Strictly speaking, the experiment estimates the effect of receiving an email signed Santiago or Gabriela Martinez rather than Brett or Emily Smith, whatever those names conveyed to the officials who read them. The claim, however, speaks of "Hispanic housing applicants", and the step from the names to ethnicity depends on what the names convey, a question of measurement that the design alone cannot settle.

## 5. Comparing among replies {#sec-posttreatment}

A greeting exists only where a reply exists, which makes the tone of a reply a more delicate outcome than the reply itself. Since the names were assigned at random to the authorities, the authorities that received each name are alike in expectation, whereas the replies were not assigned at all. If the name changes whether an official replies, the officials who answered Santiago need not resemble those who answered Brett, and a comparison of greetings among the replies then mixes the effect of the name on how officials write with a difference in which officials wrote. Conditioning an analysis on a variable that the treatment can change is known as post-treatment conditioning, and it can produce a difference between the groups even where the treatment has no effect on the outcome [@MontgomeryEtAl2018HowConditioningPosttreatment]. @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias set out the problem for audit experiments, in which the content of replies is a common outcome.

The original authors were aware of the problem, and their footnote to the result on tone reads: "As above, we also did this analysis coding all non-responses as unfriendly responses to address the truncation problem. This does not affect the results." (p. 18, note 11). The supporting information refers to the problem as the "truncation by death (non response)" problem (p. 44), a term borrowed from medical statistics, in which an outcome such as a patient's quality of life exists only for the patients who survive to be asked. In the present case, the greeting exists only for the emails that drew a reply. The two comparisons described in the footnote yield different numbers, as @tbl-two-comparisons shows.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-two-comparisons
#| tbl-cap: "The gap in named greetings between Hispanic and white names, counted among the coded replies and among all delivered emails, an email without a reply counting as one without a named greeting. Differences in proportions with HC2 tests. Source: `data/display_outcomes.csv`."
#| code-fold: true
outcomes |>
  datawizard::data_filter(contrast == "hispanic" & outcome %in% c("reply", "named", "named_any")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    Outcome = unname(c(reply = "Any reply, among delivered emails",
                       named = "Greeted by name, among coded replies",
                       named_any = "Greeted by name, among delivered emails")[outcome]),
    `Gap (points)` = fmt(b_pp), SE = fmt(se_pp, 2), p = pe(p), Emails = format(n, big.mark = ",")
  ) |>
  datawizard::data_select(c("Outcome", "Gap (points)", "SE", "p", "Emails")) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 2:5, align = "r")
```

Among the replies the gap is `r fmt(out("named", "hispanic", "b_pp"))` points, and among all delivered emails `r fmt(out("named_any", "hispanic", "b_pp"))` points. Both gaps are significant, and the footnote is right in stating that the conclusion stands, although the two numbers answer two different questions. Counting every delivered email preserves the groups exactly as randomisation made them, and the gap is thus an effect of the name on receiving a reply that opens with the name, an outcome combining whether a reply came with how it began. The comparison among replies, by contrast, addresses the question posed by the claim, which concerns the tone of the replies that came, and it corresponds to a pure effect of the name only if the name did not change who replied.

A bound can establish how far a change in who replied could go towards explaining the gap among replies. Emails with Hispanic names drew a reply `r fmt(abs(out("reply", "hispanic", "b_pp")))` points less often than emails with white names. Suppose that no official would reply to Santiago but ignore Brett's identical email, meaning that the name can only discourage a reply. The replies to white names then include a small share from officials who would not have answered a Hispanic name. The comparison of interest, among the officials who would have replied to either name, can be bounded by removing that share from the replies to white names in the two most extreme ways, once taking out only the replies that greeted by name and once only those that did not.

```{r}
#| label: trim-bound
# The trimming bounds of Lee (2009), from attrition (Coppock, Gerber, Green and
# Kern): every delivered email to a Hispanic or a white name, a reply with a
# greeting code counting as a response, and the Hispanic name assumed only to
# discourage a reply, so that the replies to white names are trimmed
delivered <- housing |>
  datawizard::data_filter(!is.na(reply) & group %in% c("white", "hispanic")) |>
  datawizard::data_modify(
    hisp = as.integer(group == "hispanic"),
    responded = as.integer(reply == 1 & !is.na(named)),
    greeted = dplyr::if_else(responded == 1, named, NA_real_)
  )
lee <- attrition::estimator_trim(Y = greeted, Z = hisp, R = responded,
                                 monotonicity = "treatment_decreases_response", se = "none",
                                 data = delivered)
extra_share <- lee[["Q"]]
bound <- 100 * c(near_zero = lee[["estimate_upper"]], far_from_zero = lee[["estimate_lower"]])
round(c(extra_share = 100 * extra_share, bound), 1)
```

About `r fmt(100 * extra_share)`% of the replies to white names would be removed, and the gap among the officials who would have replied to either name lies between `r fmt(bound[["far_from_zero"]])` and `r fmt(bound[["near_zero"]])` points, before any allowance for chance. Since even the end nearest zero is a large gap, a change in who replied cannot by itself account for the finding, provided that the assumption holds. That assumption cannot be checked in the data, which is why the specification curve retains both comparisons and why the [causal-graphs module](dags.qmd#sec-case) works through the same problem as a graph.

The second recipe incorporates the difference in replies, `r insight::format_value(mean(delivered$reply[delivered$group == "hispanic"]), as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)` for the Hispanic names against `r insight::format_value(mean(delivered$reply[delivered$group == "white"]), as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)` for the white names, into the declaration of section 3, with the result that the name changes who replies as well as how a reply begins. Authorities with a low value of `v` reply to either name, while a band of authorities, `r insight::format_value(mean(delivered$reply[delivered$group == "white"]) - mean(delivered$reply[delivered$group == "hispanic"]), as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)` of them, replies only to a white name. How these marginal repliers greet a white name cannot be recovered from the data, because their replies to white names are indistinguishable from those of the other officials. The recipe therefore sets this greeting in three ways, as never by name, as often as the other officials or always by name.

```{r}
#| label: declare-reply
reply_white <- mean(delivered$reply[delivered$group == "white"])
reply_hisp <- mean(delivered$reply[delivered$group == "hispanic"])
greet_marginal <- greet_white

reply_design <-
  DeclareDesign::declare_model(
    N = n_delivered,
    v = runif(N), u = runif(N),
    always = v < reply_hisp,
    R_Z_0 = as.integer(v < reply_white), R_Z_1 = as.integer(v < reply_hisp),
    G_Z_0 = dplyr::if_else(always, as.integer(u < greet_white), as.integer(u < greet_marginal)),
    G_Z_1 = as.integer(u < greet_hisp),
    A_Z_0 = R_Z_0 * G_Z_0, A_Z_1 = R_Z_1 * G_Z_1
  ) +
  DeclareDesign::declare_inquiry(gap_always = mean(G_Z_1[always] - G_Z_0[always]),
                                 gap_all = mean(A_Z_1 - A_Z_0)) +
  DeclareDesign::declare_assignment(Z = randomizr::complete_ra(N, m = n_hispanic)) +
  DeclareDesign::declare_measurement(R = fabricatr::reveal_outcomes(R ~ Z),
                                     G = fabricatr::reveal_outcomes(G ~ Z),
                                     A = fabricatr::reveal_outcomes(A ~ Z)) +
  DeclareDesign::declare_estimator(G ~ Z, .method = estimatr::lm_robust, se_type = "HC2",
                                   subset = R == 1, inquiry = "gap_always", term = "Z",
                                   label = "among replies") +
  DeclareDesign::declare_estimator(A ~ Z, .method = estimatr::lm_robust, se_type = "HC2",
                                   inquiry = "gap_all", term = "Z", label = "all delivered")
```

```r
DeclareDesign::redesign(reply_design, greet_marginal = c(0, greet_white, 1)) |>
  DeclareDesign::diagnose_design(sims = 2000)
```

The design poses two questions, the first concerning the effect of the name on the greeting among the authorities that would reply to either name, and the second the effect of the name on whether an email receives a named greeting at all, counted over every delivered email. The first question is answered by the comparison among replies and the second by the comparison among all delivered emails, the two questions being the estimands between which the specification curve of the case study chooses (the [multiverse module](multiverse.qmd#sec-forks) explains how much of the curve is attributable to that choice).

```{r}
#| label: tbl-reply
#| echo: false
#| tbl-cap: "The two comparisons over 2,000 simulated experiments under each assumption about the authorities that reply only to white names. Estimands and estimates in percentage points; the bias is the mean estimate minus the estimand, and the coverage the share of 95% intervals that contain the estimand. Source: `companion/_model-outputs/sim_housing_diagnosis.csv`."
reply_dx |>
  datawizard::data_arrange(c("greet_marginal", "estimator")) |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    `Marginal repliers greet a white name by name` = dplyr::case_when(
      greet_marginal == 0 ~ "never", greet_marginal == 1 ~ "always",
      .default = paste("as the others,", insight::format_value(greet_marginal, as_percent = TRUE, digits = 0))),
    Comparison = estimator,
    Estimand = sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean_estimand)),
    `Mean estimate` = sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * mean_estimate)),
    Bias = sub("^-", "−", sprintf("%.1f", 100 * bias)),
    Coverage = insight::format_value(coverage, as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)
  ) |>
  tinytable::tt() |>
  tinytable::style_tt(j = 3:6, align = "r")
```

Of the three recipes, the comparison among replies recovers the effect on the authorities that reply to either name in only one, the recipe in which the marginal repliers greet a white name as the other officials do. If the marginal repliers never greet by name, the replies to white names contain more unnamed greetings than the authorities that reply to either name would give, and the estimate falls short of the planted gap by `r insight::format_value(100 * reply_never$bias, digits = 1)` points on average, with an interval that covers the truth in `r insight::format_value(reply_never$coverage, as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)` of the draws. If the marginal repliers always greet by name, the estimate overshoots by `r insight::format_value(100 * abs(reply_always$bias), digits = 1)` points. No amount of data from the experiment can distinguish between the three recipes, because each produces data of the same kind. The trimming bounds presented above rest on the same premise, being computed from the observed replies as the range within which the effect on the authorities that reply to either name must lie, whatever the marginal repliers do.

The comparison among all delivered emails is unbiased in every recipe, because nothing is conditioned on after the names were assigned. Its estimand, however, shifts with the recipe, from `r insight::format_value(100 * min(reply_dx$mean_estimand[reply_dx$estimator == "all delivered"]), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` to `r insight::format_value(100 * max(reply_dx$mean_estimand[reply_dx$estimator == "all delivered"]), digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, since it adds the effect of the name on replying to its effect on the greeting. The two comparisons therefore answer different questions, and the simulation shows the price of each. The comparison among all delivered emails answers its own question exactly, although that question mixes two effects of the name, while the comparison among replies answers the narrower question about greetings only under an assumption that the data cannot test.

The paper encounters the same problem a second time, in its test of whether officials with Hispanic names treat Hispanic applicants differently. Since an official becomes known only by replying, the subgroup of replies from such officials is selected after the treatment. The original authors note that "Since the treatments were randomly assigned, in expectation, our emails should have reached Hispanic officials at equal rates in each condition allowing us to compare those that were returned" (p. 14), and the shares agree with that expectation. Officials with Hispanic names wrote `r pct(official_share$share[official_share$group == "white"])`, `r pct(official_share$share[official_share$group == "black"])` and `r pct(official_share$share[official_share$group == "hispanic"])` of the replies to white, Black and Hispanic names. Among the `r sub_("replies from officials", "n")` replies written by these officials to Hispanic and white names, the gap in greetings is `r fmt(sub_("replies from officials", "b_pp"))` points (`r pe(sub_("replies from officials", "p"))`), a comparison that answers a question different from that of the claim, on very few replies, and the specification curve excludes the subgroup.

## 6. Randomisation inference {#sec-ri}

Random assignment also supplies a test that requires no model of the errors, an idea that goes back to @Fisher1935DesignExperiments. Suppose that the name made no difference at all to any official, so that every authority would have answered exactly as it did whichever name it received. Under this hypothesis, known as the sharp null, the outcomes remain fixed and only the labels could have fallen differently, and reshuffling the names among the emails, again and again, thus yields the gaps that chance alone produces [@Ernst2004PermutationMethods]. The p-value is the share of reshuffles giving a gap at least as large as the observed one, with the observed assignment counted as one of them so that the p-value can never be zero [@PhipsonSmyth2010PermutationPValues].

```{r}
#| label: reshuffle
# ri2 reshuffles the names 1,999 times by complete random assignment, as the
# experiment assigned them, and recomputes the gap after each reshuffle
# (Gerber and Green 2012, chapter 3); statmod::permp() turns the number of
# reshuffles at least as extreme into the p-value of Phipson and Smyth (2010)
all_emails <- spec_frame(housing, comparison = "white", population = "all", uncoded = "drop")
set.seed(20261025)
among_replies <- ri2::conduct_ri(y ~ hisp, assignment = "hisp",
                                 declaration = randomizr::declare_ra(N = nrow(frame), m = sum(frame$hisp)),
                                 sharp_hypothesis = 0, IPW = FALSE, data = frame, sims = 1999)
set.seed(20261025)
among_delivered <- ri2::conduct_ri(y ~ hisp, assignment = "hisp",
                                   declaration = randomizr::declare_ra(N = nrow(all_emails), m = sum(all_emails$hisp)),
                                   sharp_hypothesis = 0, IPW = FALSE, data = all_emails, sims = 1999)
extreme_replies <- round(summary(among_replies)$two_tailed_p_value * 1999)
extreme_delivered <- round(summary(among_delivered)$two_tailed_p_value * 1999)
p_replies <- statmod::permp(extreme_replies, nperm = 1999, n1 = sum(frame$hisp), n2 = sum(frame$hisp == 0))
p_delivered <- statmod::permp(extreme_delivered, nperm = 1999,
                              n1 = sum(all_emails$hisp), n2 = sum(all_emails$hisp == 0))
c(replies = p_replies, delivered = p_delivered)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-reshuffle
#| fig-cap: "The gap in named greetings between Hispanic and white names after each of 1,999 random reshuffles of the names, among the coded replies (left) and among all delivered emails (right). The burgundy line marks the observed gap."
#| fig-alt: "Two histograms centred on zero. Among the replies the reshuffled gaps spread from about −15 to +15 points and the observed gap of −20 lies beyond them; among all delivered emails they spread more narrowly and the observed gap of −13 lies beyond them."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 2.8
#| code-fold: true
dplyr::bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(comparison = "among coded replies", gap = 100 * among_replies$sims_df$est_sim,
                 observed = 100 * among_replies$sims_df$est_obs),
  tibble::tibble(comparison = "among delivered emails", gap = 100 * among_delivered$sims_df$est_sim,
                 observed = 100 * among_delivered$sims_df$est_obs)
) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = gap)) +
  ggplot2::geom_histogram(binwidth = 1, fill = "#c9d1d9", colour = "white", boundary = 0) +
  ggplot2::geom_vline(ggplot2::aes(xintercept = observed), colour = "#8b1538", linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggplot2::facet_wrap(ggplot2::vars(comparison)) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) sub("^-", "−", x)) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(xlim = c(-25, 25)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "gap after reshuffling the names (points)", y = "reshuffles") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

Among the replies, `r extreme_replies` of the 1,999 reshuffles give a gap as large as the observed one, which yields p = `r fmt(p_replies, 4)`, and among all delivered emails `r extreme_delivered` do, which yields p = `r fmt(p_delivered, 4)`, the smallest value that 1,999 reshuffles can give. The two tests differ in one respect, which relates to the problem discussed in section 5. Reshuffling the names among all delivered emails repeats exactly the random assignment of the design. Reshuffling the names among the replies, on the other hand, treats the set of replies as fixed, which is correct under the sharp null, since a name that changes nothing changes no reply either, although the replies do not form a set fixed by the design. The specification curve stores a randomisation p-value of this kind for each of its `r nrow(curve)` specifications as a check, the largest of these p-values being `r fmt(max(curve$p_ri), 4)`.

## 7. Power and the replication {#sec-power}

The power of a study is the probability that it detects an effect of a given size at the chosen threshold. Power depends on the size of the effect, on the number of observations and on how variable the outcome is, the variability of a 0/1 outcome following from the share itself. For a difference between two proportions, the power can be obtained from a formula, while simulation arrives at the same quantity by counting, declaring the design with a planted gap, running it many times and counting the share of runs in which the test rejects. The script `simulate_housing.R` performs this count for gaps of 0 to 25 points below a white rate of 61%, with 1,000 runs for each gap and size. @fig-power-curves sets the comparison reported in the paper, with about 181 coded replies in each group, against the 738 replies analysed by the replication, split equally, with the power from the formula drawn as lines and the share of rejections in the simulated runs as points.

```{r}
#| label: fig-power-curves
#| fig-cap: "The power of a two-sided test at the 5% level to detect a gap in named greetings, below a share of 61% for the white names, for the comparison among the replies of the original study (181 a group) and for the 738 replies of the replication (369 a group): the analytic power of a test of two proportions (lines) and the share of 1,000 simulated experiments in which the HC2 test rejected a gap of zero (points). Sources: `data/display_power.csv` and `companion/_model-outputs/sim_housing_diagnosis.csv`."
#| fig-alt: "Two rising power curves; the replication curve lies above the original at every gap, and both approach 1 by a gap of 20 points. The simulated points, drawn as circles, lie on or very near the curves, and at a gap of zero they sit near 5%."
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
#| code-fold: true
power |>
  datawizard::data_modify(design = dplyr::if_else(startsWith(design, "original"), "original study", "replication")) |>
  ggplot2::ggplot(ggplot2::aes(x = gap_pp, y = power, colour = design)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(
    data = datawizard::data_modify(power_dx, design = dplyr::if_else(n_per_group == 181, "original study", "replication")),
    ggplot2::aes(x = 100 * gap), size = 2.2, shape = 1, stroke = 0.9
  ) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(`original study` = "#1d2733", replication = "#1f5fa8"), name = NULL) +
  ggplot2::coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 1)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "gap in named greetings (percentage points)", y = "power") +
  ggplot2::theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  ggplot2::theme(panel.grid.minor = ggplot2::element_blank(), legend.position = "top")
```

```{r}
#| label: power-80
#| include: false
# The gap below a white share of 61% at which each design reaches a power of
# 0.8. power.prop.test() solves for a second share above the first, and the
# variance p(1 - p) is the same at p and at 1 - p, so the gap below 61% equals
# the gap above 39%.
gap_80 <- purrr::map_dbl(c(original = "original", replication = "replication"), \(d) {
  n <- max(power$n_per_group[startsWith(power$design, d)])
  100 * (stats::power.prop.test(n = n, p1 = 0.39, power = 0.8)$p2 - 0.39)
})
```

The original comparison has a power of `r fmt(pw("original", 20), 2)` for a gap of 20 points, but only `r fmt(pw("original", 10), 2)` for a gap of 10 points, the near end of the published confidence interval, against `r fmt(pw("replication", 10), 2)` for the replication. Put the other way round, the original comparison reaches a power of 0.8, the usual target in the planning of a study, only for a gap of `r fmt(gap_80[["original"]])` points, and the replication for a gap of `r fmt(gap_80[["replication"]])` points. The preregistration of the replication states that its first round "achieves 90% power to detect 75% of the original effect size", following the guidelines of the Social Sciences Replication Project.

The simulated points lie close to the analytic curves, the difference remaining within what 1,000 runs produce by chance at every gap but one. At that one gap, 10 points at the size of the original study, the simulated share lies about two and a half standard errors of a share from 1,000 runs above the curve. Close agreement of this kind is what a check by simulation ought to find when the formula fits the design. At a planted gap of zero the share of rejections is the rate of false positives, `r insight::format_value(power_null$power[power_null$n_per_group == 181], as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)` at the original size and `r insight::format_value(power_null$power[power_null$n_per_group == 369], as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)` at the size of the replication. With 1,000 runs a share of about 5% is uncertain by about 0.7 points either way. The test at the size of the replication thus keeps to its level of 5%, while the test at the original size, with few replies in each group, may reject slightly less often than it promises.

Randomisation inference, carried out with ri2 in section 6, builds a distribution of the same kind from the observed data without any recipe, retaining the outcomes and reshuffling the names so that every reshuffle is a draw from a world in which the names changed nothing. The simulation at a gap of zero writes that world down as a recipe instead, and the two procedures agree because both describe what a design of this size produces when there is nothing to find.

Modest power has a second consequence, which bears on the size of a published effect. Since the standard error of the gap in the original comparison is `r fmt(ref$se_pp, 2)` points, an estimate has to exceed about `r fmt(sig_threshold)` points before it becomes significant at 5%. If the true gap were 10 points, a study of this size would reach significance about half the time, and its significant estimates would on average be larger than the truth.

```{r}
#| label: exaggeration
# The design analysis of Gelman and Carlin (2014), from retrodesign: the power,
# the chance of a significant estimate with the wrong sign (type S) and the
# factor by which a significant estimate exaggerates the truth (type M), for
# a true gap of 10 points at the standard error of the reference comparison
set.seed(20261025)
design_10 <- retrodesign::retrodesign(10, ref$se_pp, df = ref$df, n.sims = 1e5)
round(unlist(design_10), 3)
```

Under a true gap of 10 points, the significant estimates average about `r fmt(-10 * design_10$type_m)` points, and the simulated runs show the same exaggeration. At that gap the original design rejects in `r insight::format_value(power_10$power, as_percent = TRUE, digits = 1)` of the runs, while the estimates of the runs that reach significance average `r insight::format_value(100 * power_10$mean_estimate_significant, digits = 1, style_negative = "minus")` points, `r insight::format_value(power_10$mean_estimate_significant / power_10$mean_estimand - 1, as_percent = TRUE, digits = 0)` larger than the truth. A literature that publishes significant results from studies of this size therefore tends to report effects larger than those that a replication will find, even when every study is carried out correctly. This is arguably one reason why the replication, with larger samples and new names, can find a much smaller gap without either study being wrong, although this reasoning cannot show which of the many differences between the two studies is responsible. The logistic coefficient of 0.098 reported by the replication corresponds to a gap of at most `r fmt(score_max_pp, 2)` points in favour of the Hispanic names, since a logistic coefficient shifts a probability by at most a quarter of its value. The replication is set beside the specification curve on the [background page](../background.qmd#sec-replication).

## 8. Blocked randomisation {#sec-blocking}

The paper describes the assignment of the names in the single sentence quoted in section 2 (p. 8), with a footnote adding that the emails were sent on two separate days because of the batching limits of Google Mail (p. 8, note 4). Neither the paper nor the public file describes any grouping of the authorities before the names were drawn, and as the six names went out between `r sent_range[1]` and `r sent_range[2]` times, the groups were not of equal size either. The reshuffles of section 6 therefore treat the assignment as complete random assignment of the numbers of each name produced by the experiment, the closest description of the design permitted by the published record.

The replication was designed differently, its preregistration stating: "We will block randomize within each U.S. state to ensure that there is an equivalent number of Hispanic and white names contacting the housing agencies within each state." Blocking, also known as stratified randomisation, divides the units into groups on a characteristic recorded before the experiment and assigns the treatment at random within each group, in fixed numbers, so that the characteristic is balanced between the treatment groups by design rather than only in expectation. @ImaiEtAl2008MisunderstandingsExperimentalistsObservationalists, who recall the maxim of Box and colleagues, "block what you can and randomize what you cannot", put the advantage precisely: "randomization without blocking is incapable of achieving what blocking can, which is to eliminate one component of estimation error entirely" (p. 493), the component due to imbalance on the blocking variable. @AtheyImbens2017EconometricsRandomizedExperiments go further, recommending that experimenters "always stratify as much as possible, up to the point that each stratum contains at least two treated and two control units", since "committing to stratification can only improve precision, not lower it" (section 7). What blocking secures, in other words, is precision, and only in proportion to how well the blocking variable predicts the outcome, while it removes no bias, because random assignment has already done so.

A blocked experiment is analysed block by block, the gap being estimated within each block and the block gaps averaged with weights proportional to the size of each block [@AtheyImbens2017EconometricsRandomizedExperiments, section 6.1], a calculation performed by `estimatr::difference_in_means()` when it is given the blocks. The assignment itself is drawn by `randomizr::block_ra()`, and a randomisation test reshuffles the treatment within each block, as the design did, a reshuffle carried out by ri2 when the declaration made with `randomizr::declare_ra()` names the blocks. The chunk below draws, for illustration only, the kind of assignment that a blocked version of the original experiment could have used, with the six names spread evenly within the two kinds of address.

```{r}
#| label: block-ra
set.seed(20261105)
blocked_names <- randomizr::block_ra(blocks = housing$hard_email,
                                     conditions = c("Tyrone", "Shanice", "Santiago", "Gabriela", "Brett", "Emily"))
table(hard_email = housing$hard_email, name = blocked_names)
```

What a blocked analysis would and would not have changed can be shown with the original experiment. The hard-to-find address is the one characteristic in the public file that was recorded for every authority before the emails went out and that predicts the greeting. The chunk below therefore analyses the reference comparison within the two blocks formed by the address, as if the names had been blocked on it, an analysis known as post-stratification when it is applied to a design that was not blocked.

```{r}
#| label: post-stratified
frame |>
  datawizard::data_summary(replies = n(), hispanic_share = 100 * mean(hisp), by = "hard_email")
frame |>
  datawizard::data_summary(named_share = 100 * mean(y), by = c("hard_email", "group"))

blocked_fits <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  estimatr::difference_in_means(y ~ hisp, data = frame) |> estimatr::tidy(),
  estimatr::difference_in_means(y ~ hisp, blocks = hard_email, data = frame) |> estimatr::tidy()
) |>
  dplyr::mutate(analysis = c("ignoring the address", "within the two kinds of address"),
                gap = 100 * estimate, se = 100 * std.error)
blocked_fits |> dplyr::select("analysis", "gap", "se") |> dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(c("gap", "se"), \(x) round(x, 2)))

# The reshuffles of section 6, once by complete random assignment and once
# within the two kinds of address, with as many Hispanic names in each as the
# experiment gave them
block_m <- frame |> datawizard::data_summary(m = sum(hisp), by = "hard_email")
set.seed(20261105)
ri_complete <- ri2::conduct_ri(y ~ hisp, assignment = "hisp",
                               declaration = randomizr::declare_ra(N = nrow(frame), m = sum(frame$hisp)),
                               sharp_hypothesis = 0, IPW = FALSE, data = frame, sims = 1999)
set.seed(20261105)
ri_blocked <- ri2::conduct_ri(y ~ hisp, assignment = "hisp",
                              declaration = randomizr::declare_ra(blocks = frame$hard_email, block_m = block_m$m),
                              sharp_hypothesis = 0, data = frame, sims = 1999)
spread <- 100 * c(complete = stats::sd(ri_complete$sims_df$est_sim), blocked = stats::sd(ri_blocked$sims_df$est_sim))
round(spread, 2)
```

```{r}
#| label: block-values
#| include: false
block_shares <- frame |> datawizard::data_summary(hispanic_share = 100 * mean(hisp), by = "hard_email")
block_named <- frame |>
  datawizard::data_filter(group == "white") |>
  datawizard::data_summary(named_share = 100 * mean(y), by = "hard_email")
```

White names were greeted by name in `r pct(block_named$named_share[1])` of the replies from authorities with an address that could be found quickly and in `r pct(block_named$named_share[2])` of those from the other authorities, which confirms that the address does predict the greeting. Yet the analysis within the two blocks shifts the gap only from `r fmt(blocked_fits$gap[1], 2)` to `r fmt(blocked_fits$gap[2], 2)` points, and its standard error from `r fmt(blocked_fits$se[1], 3)` to `r fmt(blocked_fits$se[2], 3)`, because the random assignment of the names happened to give the two blocks almost the same share of Hispanic names among their replies, `r pct(block_shares$hispanic_share[1])` and `r pct(block_shares$hispanic_share[2])`, leaving nothing to correct. A blocked design would have guaranteed that balance instead of leaving it to chance, and the reshuffles indicate what such a guarantee is worth. Under blocking, the standard deviation of the gaps produced by chance alone would have fallen from `r fmt(spread[["complete"]], 2)` to `r fmt(spread[["blocked"]], 2)` points, by about `r fmt(100 * (1 - spread[["blocked"]] / spread[["complete"]]), 0)`%. A blocked design would, on the other hand, have estimated the same gap and removed no bias, since there was none to remove, and it would have left the problem of section 5 untouched, because blocking acts on the assignment of the emails, whereas the comparison made in the claim is among the replies, which no design assigns.

The replication cannot be reanalysed by its blocks, because its de-identified file records no state, and the analyses presented in its report, the logit with covariates and the preregistered linear probability model, include no term for the states either. When every state receives the two groups of names in equal numbers, the difference in means that ignores the states equals the average of the differences within the states, and the estimate obtained by the replication is thus the blocked estimate in all but name. The standard error of that estimate, as a rule, forgoes the precision added by the blocks rather than overstating it. An analysis using the blocks would have estimated the gap in the replication a little more precisely, and no differently.

## 9. The ethics of deception {#sec-ethics}

An audit study deceives the people whom it studies, and the officials who answered Santiago Martinez spent their working time on a request from someone who did not exist, without ever learning that their reply was data. The original authors devote a section of the paper to these costs (pp. 11–12), explaining that they contacted "government employees in their professional capacity" and that the emails were "not designed to alter their behavior but rather to measure it". The authors were "attentive to minimizing the amount of time workers devoted to requests for information from fictitious constituents" and wrote the question in such a way that a link or a pasted paragraph would answer it. The authors also report that "we did not engage with housing officials at all after the first email, even if our putative request for assistance was met with a followup question". On the deception itself the authors write: "This deception is necessary to experimentally test whether bureaucrats exhibit racial biases in their responses to constituents. Without the random assignment of race and gender, we would be unable to measure this important quantity of interest." The same passage adds that "all of our analyses reflect comparisons across groups of housing officials".

The publication of the data raises a second question, concerning the people who were studied without their consent. The ReadMe file accompanying the original authors' replication package explains that "Whether or not a housing official responded, particularly to an ostensible minority applicant, is very sensitive and potentially harmful information". The public file therefore reports the size, the composition and the poverty of each community only as thirds, so that no authority can be identified. The replication followed the same rule: "Due to Institutional Review Board restrictions, the publicly available dataset will include only the tercile version of the demographic covariates to minimize likelihood of identifying subjects." The course works only with the blinded file and makes no attempt to recover the identity of any authority. In research of this kind replication has a cost of its own, since the replication sent `r format(3050, big.mark = ",")` further fictitious requests to offices of the same kind, and a decision to replicate an audit study weighs that burden against what a second answer is worth.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Take the trimming argument of section 5 and reverse its assumption: suppose that some officials would reply to a Hispanic name but ignore an identical email from a white name, and none the other way round. Which group of replies would you trim, and in which direction would the bounds move? Then write two sentences on which of the two assumptions you find more plausible for housing officials, and what evidence in the paper bears on it.
:::

## Sources and further reading {#sec-sources}

The design of the experiment is described in the paper by the original authors [@EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect], whose accepted manuscript is openly available at [OpenBU](https://hdl.handle.net/2144/37826), and the data in its replication package on the Harvard Dataverse ([doi:10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU](https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/1HOVTU)). The literature on audit and correspondence studies cited above extends from @Pager2003MarkCriminalRecord and @BertrandMullainathan2004AreEmilyGreg to the meta-analysis by @QuillianEtAl2017MetaanalysisFieldExperiments, and in political science from @ButlerBroockman2011PoliticiansRaciallyDiscriminate to @WhiteEtAl2015WhatNeedVote. @Gaddis2017HowBlackAre examines names as treatments, while post-treatment conditioning in experiments is treated by @MontgomeryEtAl2018HowConditioningPosttreatment and, for audit studies, by @Coppock2019AvoidingPosttreatmentBias. Randomisation inference goes back to @Fisher1935DesignExperiments, with @Ernst2004PermutationMethods providing an introduction and @PhipsonSmyth2010PermutationPValues addressing the p-value. Blocking is defended by @ImaiEtAl2008MisunderstandingsExperimentalistsObservationalists, and the analysis of blocked experiments is presented by @AtheyImbens2017EconometricsRandomizedExperiments. The replication, its preregistration and its final report are available on the OSF at [osf.io/2ug8x](https://osf.io/2ug8x/). The course files behind the numbers are `housing_emails.csv`, `display_names.csv`, `display_outcomes.csv`, `display_subgroups.csv`, `display_power.csv` and `spec_curve.csv` in `data/`, each with a codebook.

For the habit of fake-data simulation, *Regression and Other Stories* is the core text, with short fake-data simulations that recur throughout and build on one another [@GelmanEtAl2020RegressionOtherStories], and *Active Statistics* packages the same moves as classroom activities [@GelmanVehtari2024ActiveStatisticsStories]. For declaring a design before the data exist and diagnosing it by simulation, the documentation of DeclareDesign works through experiments, surveys and observational designs in the four parts used in sections 3 and 5 [@BlairEtAl2023DeclareDesignDeclareDiagnose]. For multilevel structures, DeBruine and Barr build a mixed-effects simulation from scratch and recover its parameters, on the argument that constructing the data is how you come to understand the model [@DeBruineBarr2021UnderstandingMixedeffectsModels]. For simulation inside a modelling workflow – prior and posterior predictive checking, calibration, experimentation on synthetic data before touching the real thing – the Bayesian workflow book is the current statement [@GelmanEtAl2026BayesianWorkflow], and its habits arguably transfer well beyond Bayesian settings. And for simulation as a research method in its own right, the design framework of @MorrisEtAl2019UsingSimulationStudies supplies the vocabulary (aims, data-generating mechanisms, estimands, methods and performance measures, stated before the study is run), and the book-length treatment written for social scientists is @CarseyHarden2014MonteCarloSimulation.

Simulation studies are themselves analyses, with researcher degrees of freedom of their own – conditions, performance measures, which results get reported – and a comparative study can thus be tuned until any method looks superior [@PawelEtAl2024PitfallsPotentialsSimulation]. The disciplines to which this course repeatedly returns, preregistered designs and justified choices, apply to simulated data as much as to real data. The script behind every diagnosis on this page, `companion/_model-outputs/simulate_housing.R`, is committed beside the two files that it wrote, `sim_housing_diagnosis.csv` and `sim_housing_draws.csv`, and the declarations of sections 3 and 5 run when the page is built. The quickest place to begin is therefore the Try it of section 3: change what the recipe plants, run it again, and check what the estimator does when you already know the answer.
